parts:
Hi all,

I recently started to use Stan for differnt models I have been trying to fit. Basically, I am interested in building a regression model from the scratch adding all kinds of additional information/complexity. The manual, this list and all that can be found especially on github have been incredibly helpful to get things running and get first results. So right now I am a little stuck at fitting a multilevel regression model. It's repeated mesaures data recorded from a a group of 12 subjects and the outcome is the log-transformed amplitude of a signal. This signal (muscle recordings of the arm) was recorded while we put an electrode at very specific parts of the brain, so that the only predictor is the distance towards this target in mm. Everything works fine when I code model with complete pooling or another one with partial pooling, that is the one with the slope/intercept varying per subject. The problem arises when I want to incorporate a group-level predictor (in this case a single number between 1-5 which describes the amount of electrodes used at the brain for the specific subject "s"). I basically copied (and modified) the code from the pystan example with the radon contamination (originally from Gelman and Hill 2006). This is the code:

data{
int<lower=0> N; //number of total observations
int<lower=1> J; //number of subjects
int<lower=1,upper=J> s[N]; // suject ID
int<lower=1> K; // sum intercept + slope(s)
vector[J] e; // group-level interactions, number of electrodes

vector[N] y; // outcome variable
vector[N] x; // predictor(s)
}

transformed data{
// Data are z-transformed
vector[N] x_std;
vector[N] y_std;
x_std = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x);
y_std = (y - mean(y)) / sd(y);
}

parameters{
real betamu_std[K]; // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2]
real<lower=0> sigma_y_std; // total error
vector[K] e_betaj[J];
vector[K] sigma_j;
vector[K] gamma; // gamma is the random part of the group-level predictor for the slope
}

transformed parameters{
vector[N] yhat; //
vector[J] beta_std[K]; // number of beta vectors with group-level interaction
vector[J] beta_raw[K]; // number of beta vectors without group-level interaction
vector[J] beta[K]; // number of (back-transformed) beta vectors

real betamu[K]; // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2]
real<lower=0> sigma_y; // (back)-transformed error

for(j in 1:J) {
for(k in 1:K) {
beta_raw[k,j] = betamu_std[k] + sigma_b[k] *e_betaj[j,k];
beta_std[k,j] = beta_raw[k,j] + e[s[n]] * gamma[k];
}
}

for(n in 1:N) {
yhat[n] = beta_std[1,s[n]] + beta_std[2,s[n]] * x_std[n];
}

// Transform parameters back to original scale
for(j in 1:J) {
beta[1,j] = sd(y) * (beta_std[1,j] - beta_std[2,j] * mean(x) / sd(x)) + mean(y);
beta[2,j] = beta_std[2,j] * sd(y) / sd(x);
y_sig = sd(y) * sigma_y;
}

betamu[2] = betamu_std[2] * sd(y) / sd(x);
betamu[1] = betamu_std[1] * sd(y) + mean(y) - betamu_std[2] * mean(x) * sd(y) / sd(x);
}

model{
//Priors
sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
betamu_std ~ normal(0,5);
gamma ~ normal(0,1);

for(k in 1:K) {
for(j in 1:J) {
e_betaj[j,k] ~ normal(0,1);
}
}

y_std ~ student_t(4, yhat, sigma_y);
}

"

The problem is that the group-level predictor "flips" the direction of the slope from negative to positive and the checks I did to assess the model fit look really bad. I know this may be just because these group-level predictors do not add anything to the model fit but because I don't trust (yet) my model definition I wanted to know if the way I am coding especially for beta_raw and beta_std make sense at all. I am grateful for every comment on the code. And thanks for the great work you guys do.
Best


David

I don't quite follow what you're doing with the code for
multilevel regression (we'd usually put a multivariate prior
on the two variables per group---is that what your transforms are
doing?) , but there are lots of places to improve
its efficiency.

For a start, take all those expensive computations on the data
like mean(x) and sd(y) and even sd(y) / sd(x)
and do them in transformed data and store the result.

You can vectorize almost every statement in the program after
that, which will also give you speedups.

for (n in 1:N)
yhat[n] = beta_std[1,s[n]] + beta_std[2,s[n]] * x_std[n];

as

yhat = beta_std[1, s] + beta_std[2, s] .* x_std;

Won't help with efficiency, but hopefully easier to read and digest.

And you can vectorize this:

for (k in 1:K)
for (j in 1:J) {
e_betaj[j,k] ~ normal(0,1);

by declaring e_betaj as a matrix as:

to_vector(e_beta) ~ normal(0, 1);

This

for(j in 1:J) {
for(k in 1:K) {
beta_raw[k,j] = betamu_std[k] + sigma_b[k] *e_betaj[j,k];
beta_std[k,j] = beta_raw[k,j] + e[s[n]] * gamma[k];
}
}

for (j in 1:J) {
beta_raw[ , j] = betamu_sd + sigma_b .* e_betaj[j, ];
beta_std[ , j] = ...

Is K = 2? I find it hard to follow when a bound's used as a declared
data variable and hard coded. It means the program won't even work for
K != 2 and you shouldn't have K as data.

Hi Bob,

first of all, please apologise the somehow very bulky piece of code I provided in a first instance and thank you very much for your suggestions with the vectorization. I have tried to tidy up the unnecessary parts (transformation of the data and back transformation to obtain z-scores) and to apply the steps of vectorisation you proposed (although for clarity I have transformed beta to beta0 and beta1, I will probably vectorise this when I'm sure the model is right) . This is the code now:

data{
    int<lower=0> N;                     //number of total observations
    int<lower=1> J;                      //number of subjects
    int<lower=1,upper=J> s[N];     // suject ID
vector[J] e;                            // group-level interactions (number of electrodes)

vector[N] y;                           // outcome variable
    vector[N] x;                           // predictor(s)   
}

parameters{
    real beta_mu[2];                                    // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2] 
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;                         // total error
    matrix[2,J] e_betaj;
    vector<lower=0,upper=100>[2] sigma_b;   
    vector[2] gamma;                                  // random part of group-level predictors (electrode count) (?)
}
  
transformed parameters{
    vector[N] y_hat;
    vector[J] beta0_raw;
    vector[J] beta1_raw;
    vector[J] beta0;
    vector[J] beta1;

    beta0_raw = beta_mu[1] + sigma_b[1] * e_betaj[1]';
    beta1_raw = 0.1 * beta_mu[2] + sigma_b[2] * e_betaj[2]';         // why multiplying with 0.1 ?!?

    beta0 = beta0_raw + e * gamma[1];
    beta1 = beta1_raw + e * gamma[2];
   
    for (i in 1:N)
        y_hat[i] = beta0[s[i]] + beta1[s[i]] * x[i];

}
  
model {
    //Priors
    sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

beta_mu ~ normal(0, 5);
    gamma ~ normal(0,1);
    to_vector(e_betaj) ~ normal(0, 1);
   
    y ~ student_t(4, y_hat, sigma_y);
}

Unsurprisingly, it runs much faster than before, but the results remain the same. Without the group-level predictor ("e") the slope is negative while after including it, the slope is reversed and the fit of the model is a disaster. I haven't found too much on varying intercepts and slopes with group-level predictors but my hunch would be that it is not valid to include the "e * gamma"-term when there is one value of "e" per subject and it ranges from 1-5 the way I'm doing it. And it may not make much sense but I thought I run the model like this and when this works I extend it incorporating multivariate priors according to chapter 6.12 of the rstan manual as you also suggested (Although if the way I'm doing it is nonsense and it makes more sense to do it in one step, it would be of course helpful to know as well). I know these are rather basic questions and I appreciate the time you are spending. Thanks in advance.

Best
David

I've fit similar sort of models on similar types of data.

Do you have plots of the raw data (i.e., distance towards target versus signal amplitude with a linear fit for each subject, with separate facets for each count of electrodes? If not, ggplot2 is great for this). This will help considerably in deciding how the number of electrodes should be incorporated into the model. With 12 subjects you will likely have difficulty in estimating the effect of number of electrodes if estimating for each case of 1 to 5 and will need to include appropriate priors. Depending on the plot of the data, it may be appropriate to do partial pooling for the effect of the number of electrodes on intercept and slope. Alternatively, if the plot shows there is an approximately linear influence of number of electrodes on intercept and/or slope then can make some modifications of your model to hopefully get reasonable estimates.

Numerous other improvements are possible but first need to determine the appropriate structure of the model given the data.

Daniel

Thanks, the plot makes it much easier to see the form of an appropriate model.

Firstly I'd demean the log amplitude: df$logamps <- df$logamp - mean(df$logamp)

Then try this model which has some minor changes to above:

data{
    int<lower=0> N;                     //number of total observations
    int<lower=1> J;                      //number of subjects
    int<lower=1,upper=J> s[N];     // suject ID
    vector[J] e;                            // group-level interactions (number of electrodes)

    vector[N] y;                           // outcome variable
    vector[N] x;                           // predictor(s)   
}

parameters{
    real beta_mu[2];                                    // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2] 
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;                         // total error
    matrix[2,J] e_betaj;

vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_b;    
    real gamma; // effect of electrode count on slope
}
  
transformed parameters{

vector[N] y_hat;
    vector[J] beta0_raw;
    vector[J] beta1_raw;
    vector[J] beta0;
    vector[J] beta1;

    beta0_raw = beta_mu[1] + sigma_b[1] * e_betaj[1]';

beta1_raw = beta_mu[2] + sigma_b[2] * e_betaj[2]';

    beta0 = beta0_raw; // No evidence of an effect of electrode count on Intercept and given limited data exclude estimation
    beta1 = beta1_raw + e * gamma;

for (i in 1:N)
        y_hat[i] = beta0[s[i]] + beta1[s[i]] * x[i];

}
  
model {
    //Priors
    sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
beta_mu ~ normal(0, 1); // Need tighter prior

gamma ~ normal(0,1);
    to_vector(e_betaj) ~ normal(0, 1);
   
    y ~ student_t(4, y_hat, sigma_y);
}

parts:
Hi David,

Re "beta_mu [...] // Need tighter prior" than normal(0, 1)" -- it was previously normal(0,5) which is quite wide, normal(0,1) was a change I'd made and the comment was just noting why. Tighter prior helps with sampling, although need to demean data so intercept becomes closer to 0.

The model is on the right track, and can see how useful a multivariate prior is. Overall mean negative intercept and negative slope for the relationship between signal and distance matches the data.

One thing is that gamma is the opposite sign to what it should be (and can't be any other way with the constraint that gamma has a lower bound of zero ;-). As you increase the number of electrodes the plot indicates that the slope becomes more negative. Hence as I assume ec[j] is positive, gamma should be negative. Thus change to real<upper=0> for gamma. A negative gamma can be interpreted as the amount that the slope becomes more negative per extra electrode, and definitely makes sense to look at. I assume the beta_raw's will be compensating for the current constraint, hence the other variable that would be useful to see is beta_raw as can match with plot to check that estimates are correct.

The results are looking promising, a few more tweaks to the model and I think will be close.

Regards,

Daniel

Thanks, the plot makes it much easier to see the form of an appropriate model.

Firstly I'd demean the log amplitude: df$logamps <- df$logamp - mean(df$logamp)

Then try this model which has some minor changes to above:

data{
    int<lower=0> N;                     //number of total observations
    int<lower=1> J;                      //number of subjects
    int<lower=1,upper=J> s[N];     // suject ID
    vector[J] e;                            // group-level interactions (number of electrodes)

    vector[N] y;                           // outcome variable
    vector[N] x;                           // predictor(s)   
}

parameters{
    real beta_mu[2];                                    // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2] 
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;                         // total error
    matrix[2,J] e_betaj;
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_b;    
    real gamma; // effect of electrode count on slope
}
  
transformed parameters{
    vector[N] y_hat;
    vector[J] beta0_raw;
    vector[J] beta1_raw;
    vector[J] beta0;
    vector[J] beta1;

    beta0_raw = beta_mu[1] + sigma_b[1] * e_betaj[1]';
    beta1_raw = beta_mu[2] + sigma_b[2] * e_betaj[2]';

    beta0 = beta0_raw; // No evidence of an effect of electrode count on Intercept and given limited data exclude estimation
    beta1 = beta1_raw + e * gamma;
   
    for (i in 1:N)
        y_hat[i] = beta0[s[i]] + beta1[s[i]] * x[i];

}
  
model {
    //Priors
    sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    beta_mu ~ normal(0, 1); // Need tighter prior
    gamma ~ normal(0,1);
    to_vector(e_betaj) ~ normal(0, 1);
   
    y ~ student_t(4, y_hat, sigma_y);
}

Would be great if you could post the resulting inferences for sigma_y, sigma_b, beta_mu, and gamma. If still getting results that aren't sensible then making the change to a multivariate prior for the intercept and slope should hopefully fix it.
